newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FIGURE SKATING-QUADRUPLE JUMPS CONSPICUOUS BY THEIR ABSENCE.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-QUADRUPLE JUMPS CONSPICUOUS BY THEIR ABSENCE.

text.p: They have been called the men who would fly. But as Thursday's free skating final at the world championships proved, they need to strengthen their wings.
Up to 12 quadruple jumps had been predicted for the final, based on the last practice sessions, but only four materialised on the night.
One came from champion Elvis Stojko of Canada, who combined a quadruple toe loop with a triple toe loop in a repeat of the acrobatic achievement he pioneered in the Champions' final early this month.
Stojko's first quad-triple in world championship history led to his regaining the title he won in 1994 and 1995.
Two more quadruple jumps came from China's Guo Zhengxin, one with a double toe loop tacked on, the other by itself as he advanced from 22nd to 19th place with the 15th best free skating programme.
The other came from Latvian Konstantin Kostin, who finished 17th after several other mistakes in his routine.
But several other skaters who had indicated that they would attempt quads either failed with them or dropped them at the last minute.

Russian Ilya Kulik, who was successful with his in qualifying last Sunday, could manage only a triple while team mate Alexei Urmanov, the other success story from qualifying, dropped out injured just before he was due to skate.

Runner-up Todd Eldredge, despite a sprained ankle, was said to have decided in final practice to do a quadruple but did not, though he promised one for next year's Olympics. Fourth-placed Viacheslav Zagorodniuk of Ukraine also failed to do one.
The jump comprises four revolutions in the air with takeoff and landing on the same foot.
"It's one thing to do it in practice or a smaller event but it's much tougher to do at the world championships," Stojko said earlier in the week.
Stojko said he had experimented with a triple-quad combination, which would be harder with the tougher jump done second, as well as quadruples off other jumps like the salchow.
"But a quad-quad? You'd have to be absolutely perfect to pull that off," he said.
One judge, Italian Daniela Cavelli, did rate him perfect on Thursday, giving him 6.0 for technique despite some minor flaws elsewhere in his routine.

The quad toe jump was first achieved in international championships by Canadian Kurt Browning at the 1998 worlds in Budapest, though Czech Josef Sabovcik was thought by many observers to have achieved one two years earlier, only for it to be disallowed.
The jump has been achieved several more times in recent years and it is felt that next year it will be essential for success.
"Without a quad, there is going to come a time soon when you shouldn't show up," a source close to Stojko has said.
